pr_title: scope: allow unprivileged delegation on scopes
pr_body:
Previously it was possible to set delegate property for scope, but you
were not able to allow unprivileged process to manage the scope's cgroup
hierarchy. This is useful when launching manager process that  will run
unprivileged but is supposed to manage its own (scope) sub-hierarchy.

Fixes #21683
pr_comments:
@poettering PTAL

Semaphore CI failure is unrelated.

@poettering updated!

I just remembered, there is one more important thing that may need to be addressed before this is finally good to go. That is (de)serialization. I am not sure if PIDs watched by the unit are rewatched automatically after deserialisation. Not dropping "needs-rework" just yet.
(this shouldnt need serialization afaics, hence the merge)

issue_context.title: Delegation to unprivileged users doesn't work for scopes
issue_context.body:
**systemd version the issue has been seen with**
 > systemd-249

<!-- For older version please use distribution trackers (see https://systemd.io/CONTRIBUTING#filing-issues). -->

**Used distribution**
 > Fedora

**Linux kernel version used** (`uname -a`)
<!-- Make sure to enclose the pasted kernel version in `backticks`, so that
     GitHub doesn't convert the `#` character typically included in it into a
     reference to old GitHub issues. -->
 > `Linux localhost 5.16.0-0.rc3.24.fc36.x86_64 #1 SMP PREEMPT Mon Nov 29 13:43:51 UTC 2021 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux`

**CPU architecture issue was seen on**
 > x86_64

**Expected behaviour you didn't see**
> I would expect that bash process started by systemd-run is placed in a cgroup that can be managed by test user.

**Unexpected behaviour you saw**
> $subject, i.e. cgroup is owned by root user.

**Steps to reproduce the problem**
```bash
$ useradd test
$ systemd-run --uid=test -p Delegate=yes --scope --unit foo.scope --slice bar.slice /bin/bash
$ ls -ld /sys/fs/cgroup/bar.slice/foo.scope/
drwxr-xr-x. 2 root root 0 Dec  8 08:07 /sys/fs/cgroup/bar.slice/foo.scope/
```
comments: Although, it seems to me this is a bug it might be fairly difficult to fix because we would probably need to resolve the user at the time when we are starting scope unit. But, doing synchronous NSS lookups from PID1 might lead to deadlocks...
mmh but wouldn't systemd --user cover that use case? If it goes through the system manager, then it's under the system cgroup tree, no?
I guess your problem is sending the job to a _different_ user session?
You may want to run processes under non-privileged users that are system users, i.e. they never login and never have any session nor user manager running. IOW, there are no user-sessions.

Sounds like ExecStartPre=! to do the setup would work? Supporting `systemd-run --machine @1000` to run from root to a different session would be something nice to support, but arbitrary uid/gid rewriting, I'm not too sure

It was a mistake on my part to use normal user in the steps to reproduce. There should have been something like,

```bash
$ useradd --system test
```

> Sounds like ExecStartPre=! to do the setup would work?

Well, scope units don't have unit files. I mean, sure you can workaround this just fine with service units. But that is besides the point. Question is whether it should also work for scope units?
I'm not sure. The `scope` unit doesn't support a `User` setting. Perhaps it could be added? Then systemd-run would just use it.
cgroup delegation to unpriv users for scopes simply doesn't exist so far. i.e. no User/Group= setting. Sounds like something we could add though, but it would be a new feature, not a bug.

review_comments: you can drop this actually, all fields are initialized to NULL anyway initially

This hard-coded timeout looks fishy.
Couldn't this be charged against `JobRunningTimeoutSec=`? (I know it's not the same, especially diverts from service start, however, it'd reuse the existing mechanisms.)

scope_enter_chown_cgroup() expects to be called with s->user set, right?

So we should have an assert for that here.

Alternatively, move the check before the scope_enter_chown_cgroup() invocation into this function, and then make it return 0 if there's no chowning to be done, and > 0 if we are now in the chowning state.

That way, there would be only place to check the setting (i.e. inside this function) instead of two (in the caller via `if` and here via `assert()`).

up to you...

I will add an `assert()` and keep the `if` in the caller because I don't want to obscure the fact that we `chown()` the cgroup (i.e. we actually enter the state) only if delegation is turned on and `user` is set.
